Proposed radar survey could improve understanding of historic Glencarlyn cemetery

By Scott McCaffrey
Published November 16, 2026 at 2:45PM
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:19
Instaread

A new fundraiser aims to take a high-tech approach to learning more about a historic cemetery in Glencarlyn.

Members of two of the community’s most historic families, the Balls and the Carlins, were buried at the Ball-Carlin Cemetery between 1766 and 1905. After that, the grounds fell into a degree of disrepair, and according to the county records, remaining headstones were moved to a corner of the cemetery in the 1950s.

Today, headstones are not visible at the cemetery, located at 300 S. Kensington Street between the Glencarlyn branch library and the Carlin Hall community house.

A GoFundMe aims to raise $6,000 to support a survey of the cemetery using ground-penetrating radar. It has raised over $3,000 as of today (Monday).

Todd Wallace, an organizer of the effort on behalf of the Arlington Historical Society, Master Gardeners of Northern Virginia and a Glencarlyn history group, said in a Facebook post that the cemetery currently yields more questions than answers.

“We have a list of people who are supposed to be buried in the cemetery, but we don’t know if the list is complete, and we don’t know where everyone is buried or how many burials are in the cemetery,” he wrote.

The project would represent “a respectful and non-invasive way to study the cemetery without excavation or disturbing graves,” according to organizers, who added:

“This work can help determine whether the known boundaries are accurate, improve understanding of who may be buried there, and preserve an important piece of local history. Please support this effort to better understand and protect Ball-Carlin Cemetery. Every contribution will help make this research possible and help share the findings with the Glencarlyn community, the wider Arlington community and future researchers.”

Brandon Hemel, president of the Glencarlyn Civic Association, is among the project’s supporters.

“We have a great team focused on the history of Glencarlyn,” he told ARLnow. “I hope their fundraiser is successful and we can learn more about the early residents of our community.”

Absent a commemorative marker adjacent to the site, those passing by would be unlikely to know a historic burial ground was close by. The gate on the fence surrounding the site is locked, while most of the parcel is covered with either grass or plantings, including a popular destination for monarch butterflies.

John Ball was one of the first settlers in what today is Glencarlyn, receiving a 166-acre land grant from Lord Fairfax in 1742. Six years later, Moses Ball was granted 91 acres nearby.

The intertwined families acquired additional acreage in the late 1700s. In the late 1800s, they operated a resort on the current location of Glencarlyn Park.

The last person interred on the site was Mary Alexander Carlin, who was born in the area and spent most of her life there until her death in 1905.

In 1978, the site was designated a county historic district, which provides protections from encroachment or redevelopment.

Another final resting place for members of the Ball family, located on Washington Blvd in Ballston, was also designated a local historic district in 1978 and was preserved when a nearby church was redeveloped for affordable housing.

Other burial grounds designated as local historic districts include Calloway Cemetery, Mount Salvation Baptist Church Cemetery, Travers Family Graveyard and Walker Chapel & Cemetery.
